\chapter{The Eating House}
\label{ch:hi-the-eating-house}
\hlchaptermodality{80}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the place I eat, the meal, the bill and the person who brings it, and say that I eat and drink.}

Complete HI-C73-drink and say all five words in order, then say the eating-and-drinking pair and what each half can mean.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hoṭal]{\hi{होटल} (hoṭal) — an eating house}

\label{lesson:HI-C73-eating-house}



\begin{quote}
Two words back: what does \emph{mahãgā} mean, and what is \textbf{\hi{ख़रीदना}}? The next five words are for the place you buy a meal.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{होटल}}
\textbf{\hi{होटल}} (\emph{hoṭal}) — \textquotedblleft{}an eating house\textquotedblright{}.

English \emph{hotel}, and behind it Latin \emph{hospitāle}, a house for guests. The same Latin word gave English \emph{hospital} and \emph{hospitality}: one root for the place that takes a stranger in, whether to feed, to lodge or to heal.

Here is the part a dictionary will not tell you loudly enough. In everyday Hindi a \hi{होटल} is most often somewhere you \textbf{eat}, not somewhere you sleep. A small roadside place with six tables and no rooms at all calls itself a \hi{होटल}, and \textbf{\hi{चाय} \hi{होटल}} is a tea shop.

So take the word as \textquotedblleft{}eating house\textquotedblright{} first and \textquotedblleft{}hotel\textquotedblright{} second, and you will read far more signboards correctly.

The \hi{ो} is the \emph{o} matra, a single stroke above the headline with a tail.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five words for a meal you did not cook.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mahãgā}, then read \textbf{\hi{ख़रीदना}} and say what it means
  \item \emph{Hear:} \emph{hoṭal}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{hoṭal}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chāy hoṭal}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{होटल} usually mean on an Indian signboard? (A place to eat.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nāshtā]{\hi{नाश्ता} (nāshtā) — breakfast}

\label{lesson:HI-C73-breakfast}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{hoṭal}, then write \textbf{\hi{होटल}}: \hi{ह} with \hi{ो} above it, then \hi{ट}, then \hi{ल}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{नाश्ता}}
\textbf{\hi{नाश्ता}} (\emph{nāshtā}) — \textquotedblleft{}breakfast\textquotedblright{}.

Persian \ar{ناشتا} (\emph{nāshtā}) means \textquotedblleft{}not having eaten, on an empty stomach\textquotedblright{}. The meal took its name from the emptiness it ends.

English did the identical thing and nobody notices any more: \emph{breakfast} is the \textbf{breaking} of the \textbf{fast}. Two languages, no contact, the same picture — the night is a fast and the morning meal is what ends it.

The middle of the word stacks \hi{श} on \hi{त} with the vowel-killer \hi{्}, the same stack you have written in \textbf{\hi{नमस्ते}} and read in \textbf{\hi{स्टेशन}}.

\textbf{\hi{नाश्ता}} is also a doing word's companion: \textbf{\hi{नाश्ता} \hi{करना}} is \textquotedblleft{}to have breakfast\textquotedblright{}, built the way \textbf{\hi{आराम} \hi{करना}} was.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A place to eat, and the first meal of the day to eat there.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\hi{ख़रीदना}}, then say it without looking
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nāshtā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nāshtā karnā}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{होटल} once more, then \hi{नाश्ता} beside the printed model
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{नाश्ता} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}breakfast\textquotedblright{}.) What does the Persian word say about your stomach? (That it is empty.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bil]{\hi{बिल} (bil) — the bill}

\label{lesson:HI-C73-bill}



\begin{quote}
Which of your two words is the place, and which is the meal?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{बिल}}
\textbf{\hi{बिल}} (\emph{bil}) — \textquotedblleft{}the bill\textquotedblright{}.

English \emph{bill}, borrowed for the slip of paper and used for nothing else. Three letters: \hi{ब}, the \hi{ि} matra written to its left, and \hi{ल}.

Now a warning your eye needs. You already hold \textbf{\hi{बिलकुल}}, \textquotedblleft{}absolutely\textquotedblright{}, and you have met \textbf{\hi{बिल्ली}}, a cat. All three open on the same three letters and none of them is related to the others — \hi{बिलकुल} is Arabic, \hi{बिल्ली} is Sanskrit, \hi{बिल} is English. Reading the first syllable and guessing will send you to the wrong word.

\textbf{\hi{बिल} \hi{दीजिए}} asks for it, in the same polite frame that got you a ticket and a cup of tea.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: \hi{होटल}, \hi{नाश्ता}, \hi{बिल}. A place, a meal, and what arrives afterwards.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bil}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bil dījie}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{bil} and \emph{bilkul}, and say which one is a piece of paper
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you ask for the bill? (\emph{bil dījie}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[veṭar]{\hi{वेटर} (veṭar) — a waiter}

\label{lesson:HI-C73-waiter}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\hi{बिल}} from memory, remembering that the \hi{ि} goes down before the \hi{ल} it is heard after.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{वेटर}}
\textbf{\hi{वेटर}} (\emph{veṭar}) — \textquotedblleft{}a waiter\textquotedblright{}.

English \emph{waiter}, and the spelling shows two habits you have now seen three times. The English \emph{w} is written \hi{व}, because Hindi has one letter where English splits \emph{v} and \emph{w}. The English \emph{t} is written \hi{ट}, retroflex, as it was in \textbf{\hi{टिकट}} and \textbf{\hi{स्टेशन}}.

This is the word on the sign and on the pay slip, so it is the one to be able to read. Across a table it is used far less than you would expect: people catch an eye rather than call a title, and a raised hand does the work.

So hold \hi{वेटर} for reading, and expect the room itself to be quieter than the word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and the person you ask for the fourth thing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{veṭar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{hoṭal}, then \emph{veṭar}, then \emph{bil}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{वेटर}, with \hi{व} for the English w and \hi{ट} for the English t
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Hindi letter carries an English \emph{w}? (\hi{व}.) And an English \emph{t}? (\hi{ट}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pīnā]{\hi{पीना} (pīnā) — to drink}

\label{lesson:HI-C73-drink}



\begin{quote}
Name the four words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{पीना}}
\textbf{\hi{पीना}} (\emph{pīnā}) — \textquotedblleft{}to drink\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \hi{पिबति} (\emph{pibati}), \textquotedblleft{}drinks\textquotedblright{}, from a root so old that Latin \emph{bibere}, \textquotedblleft{}to drink\textquotedblright{}, is the same word wearing different clothes. English \emph{potion} and \emph{potable} come down the Latin side of that family.

Now the pair. \textbf{\hi{खाना}} you already own as \textquotedblleft{}food\textquotedblright{} — and \hi{खाना} is \textbf{also} \textquotedblleft{}to eat\textquotedblright{}, exactly as \hi{गाना} was both the song and the singing. Put them together and Hindi has one of its most-used pairs:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{खाना}} — food, and to eat. \textbf{\hi{पीना}} — to drink.
\end{quote}

\textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{चाय} \hi{पीता} \hi{हूँ}} is \textquotedblleft{}I drink tea\textquotedblright{}, in the frame you have used all along. And \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{खाना} \hi{खाता} \hi{हूँ}} puts the word into one breath twice — once for the food, once for the eating — with nothing between them but the ending.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \hi{होटल}, \hi{नाश्ता}, \hi{बिल}, \hi{वेटर}, \hi{पीना}. A place, a meal, a bill, the person who brings it, and the two doing words that made you come in.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pīnā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{maiṁ chāy pītā hūṁ}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{khānā} as the food, and \emph{khānā} as the eating
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{पीना}, then say all five of this chapter in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{पीना} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}to drink\textquotedblright{}.) What two things can \hi{खाना} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}food\textquotedblright{}, and \textquotedblleft{}to eat\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
